This led to multiple basic and edge-case failures, including cases where the pair is not at indices [0,1] and where input handling differs from the expected behavior.

dimensions.what_to_improve: The expected approach is O(n) time with an O(n) hash map. Given nums.length up to 1e5, a naive O(n^2) solution is risky, and hardcoding is not a solution. Be prepared to state and justify O(n)/O(n) for the canonical solution.

dimensions.what_to_improve: The loop body is empty and the function returns a constant, which is not maintainable or correct. Add real logic, and return early when the pair is found; also match the platform’s expected behavior for invalid/empty input if it can occur in tests.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You did not use any hints (per the hint log).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independence here didn’t translate into a working solution. When you’re stuck, use the remaining time to implement the standard pattern rather than submitting a placeholder/hardcoded return.

thinking_and_logic: A correct Two Sum solution should iterate once through nums while tracking previously seen values in a hash map from value -> index. For each value x at index i, compute complement = target - x; if complement is already in the map, return [map[complement], i]. This guarantees you don’t use the same element twice and runs in O(n) time, which matches the constraints.
code_assessment: The submitted code is an unfinished scaffold: the for-loop contains only pass, and the function always returns [0, 1]. This directly explains the failures where the valid pair is elsewhere (e.g., expected [2,4]) and where the expected output differs for special inputs (e.g., empty input expected []). To pass, the hardcoded return must be replaced with actual complement-check logic.

next_steps.action: Implement the standard one-pass hash map solution for Two Sum from memory
next_steps.why: It is the canonical O(n) approach and avoids the common pitfall of using the same element twice.
next_steps.how: Maintain seen = {}. For i, x in enumerate(nums): if (target-x) in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; else: seen[x]=i.

next_steps.action: Practice translating constraints into complexity choices
next_steps.why: With n up to 1e5, O(n^2) is too slow; interviewers expect you to justify O(n) with hashing.
next_steps.how: For each problem, explicitly write down n and the target complexity before coding; sanity-check with n=1e5 whether your approach is feasible.

next_steps.action: Build an edge-case checklist you run before final submission
next_steps.why: The failures show mismatches on basic placement and edge cases (negatives, two elements, empty input).
next_steps.how: Before submitting, test: pair at end, negatives, duplicates (e.g., [3,3], target=6), smallest size (2), and clarify what to do if input can be empty/invalid in the platform’s tests.

patterns_to_study: avoiding reuse of the same index in pair problems
encouragement: Once you consistently reach for the hash-map complement pattern and do a quick edge-case pass before submitting, this is a problem you should be able to complete correctly in just a few minutes.
